questions.stem: Ten independent trials each have success probability 0.3. X counts successes. What makes a binomial model appropriate?
questions.explanation: Those experimental conditions define the binomial setting.
choices: The expected count is an integer.
Fixed trial count, two outcomes, independence, and constant success chance.

questions.stem: Independent tasks each succeed with probability 0.9. Which shortcut gives at least one failure among three tasks?
questions.explanation: At least one failure complements all successes.
choices: 1 minus the probability all three succeed.
1 minus the probability exactly one succeeds.

questions.stem: A population contains 4 observations with a sum of squared deviations from its mean of 36. What is the population variance?
questions.explanation: Population variance divides the sum of squared deviations by the population size: 36/4=9.

questions.stem: Compare U(0,12) and U(20,32). What is true about their standard deviations?
questions.explanation: A common shift changes center without changing spread.
choices: The first is larger because it includes zero.
The second is larger because its mean is larger.

questions.stem: A box has 3 red and 7 blue tokens; 5 are drawn without replacement. Why is 4 red impossible?
questions.explanation: The success count is bounded by available red tokens.

questions.stem: A report gives sample SD=6 minutes and SE=1 minute. Which describes variation among individual observed times?
questions.explanation: Sample SD describes observed individual spread; SE describes mean-estimation precision.

questions.stem: A fixed 5-kg container is added to a shipment of random item masses. What changes?
questions.explanation: A fixed additive quantity shifts the distribution without adding random variability.
choices: Expected total rises by 5 kg; total SD is unchanged.
Both mean and SD rise by 5 kg.

questions.stem: Students may use both laptops and tablets. Laptop use is 70%, tablet use 60%. Why is a two-slice pie chart inappropriate?
questions.explanation: Pie slices partition a whole; overlapping memberships are not such a partition.
choices: A pie chart requires exactly three categories.

questions.stem: What equation describes a continuous model's 90th percentile k?
questions.explanation: The percentile cutoff has the stated area to its left.

questions.stem: One hundred valid 95% intervals are constructed in repeated sampling. Must exactly 95 cover the mean?
questions.explanation: A long-run proportion is not an exact finite-sample quota.
choices: No; the coverage count itself can vary.
Yes; any other count proves bias.
Yes; the confidence level fixes that count.

questions.stem: Most files are small, with a few extremely large files. Which better describes a typical file's size?
questions.explanation: The median is less pulled by a few large files.

questions.stem: On a die, A is even and B is greater than 3. Which results satisfy both?
questions.explanation: The intersection contains results meeting both conditions.

questions.stem: A population is half faulty cables. A random sample of 6 is drawn without replacement. What faulty count is expected?
questions.explanation: Expected count equals sample size times population faulty fraction.

questions.stem: Daily print totals are shown in a histogram instead of a time-series graph. What information is lost?
questions.explanation: A histogram summarizes the distribution without retaining chronology.
choices: Which total occurred on which date.

questions.stem: An exponential density extends far right with diminishing height. What does that say about very long waits?
questions.explanation: An unbounded right tail allows large values without making them frequent.
choices: They must occur as often as short waits.
They are possible but less common than short waits.
They are impossible once the mean is exceeded.

questions.stem: A sample has 8 observations. Its sum of squared deviations is already supplied. Which divisor gives sample variance?
questions.explanation: Sample variance uses n-1, unlike the population calculation with all population members.

questions.stem: Population SD doubles while sample size stays fixed. What happens to SE?
questions.explanation: SE is proportional to population SD at fixed n.

questions.stem: The course uses N(mean, SD). A technician expects readings from N(40,6) to cluster near 6. What is the best correction?
questions.explanation: The first parameter is the center; the SD measures variation around it, rather than another center.
choices: They cluster near 6; 40 is the sample size.
The readings cluster near 40; 6 describes their spread.
The model allows only the two values 6 and 40.

questions.stem: A model describes the mass of one package. Is its SD automatically appropriate for the mean mass of 100 independent packages?
questions.explanation: Units can match while distributions and spreads differ.
choices: No; the average has less spread.
Yes; both are measured in grams.

questions.stem: A symmetric interval is 8 to 12. What is the margin of error?
questions.explanation: Margin of error is half the total width.

questions.stem: Population SD is known and the sample is large. What still needs checking for the usual mean interval?
questions.explanation: A known SD does not replace sampling and dependence assumptions.
choices: Whether every observation equals the mean.
Whether the mean is a whole number.

questions.stem: Mean is 30 and SD is 4. Which value has z=1.5?
questions.explanation: Add 1.5 times 4 to the mean.

questions.stem: Three reported percentages are 33.3%, 33.3%, and 33.3%. What most reasonably explains the 99.9% total?
questions.explanation: Rounding can make displayed percentages differ slightly from 100%.

questions.stem: For comparison, sample SD and confidence are held fixed while n increases. What happens to a t mean interval's margin?
questions.explanation: Larger n reduces estimated SE and increases degrees of freedom.
choices: It increases because there are more observations.
It decreases as SE and the critical t value decrease.

questions.stem: Data are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. How do mean and median compare?
questions.explanation: The values balance symmetrically around 6.
choices: The mean is below the median.

questions.stem: A fixed fee increases by 2 dollars. What happens to net-gain mean and SD?
questions.explanation: Subtracting a constant shifts all outcomes without changing their spread.
choices: Mean falls by 2; SD is unchanged.

questions.stem: P(A OR B)=0.75. What is the probability of neither?
questions.explanation: Neither is the complement of the union.

questions.stem: A supplied probability table lists P(X=0),...,P(X=8). To find P(X<=2), which entries are needed?
questions.explanation: At most 2 is a cumulative event including all counts through 2.

questions.stem: Individual masses have SD 20 g; means of 25 independent masses have SD 4 g. Which spread applies to one package?
questions.explanation: The individual distribution keeps its own SD; the mean uses a smaller SE.

questions.stem: A uniform interval centered at 10 doubles its width while keeping center 10. What happens?
questions.explanation: Uniform mean depends on midpoint; SD is proportional to width.

questions.stem: Most waits are short, but a few extend far toward large values. What determines the skew direction?
questions.explanation: Skew is named for the direction of the long tail.
choices: The long tail toward large values.
The side with the tallest bar alone.

questions.stem: The ordered data are 2, 4, 4, 7, 20. What is the median?
questions.explanation: The middle observation is the third value, 4.

questions.stem: A sum event and its equivalent mean event use correctly matched centers and SDs. How do their z-scores compare?
questions.explanation: Scaling numerator and denominator by n leaves standardization unchanged.
choices: The sum z-score is n times larger.
The mean z-score is always zero.

questions.stem: A symmetric confidence interval is 8 to 12. What point estimate is at its center?
questions.explanation: The midpoint is the estimate, not either endpoint.

questions.stem: Two distinct terminal paths describe exactly one head in two tosses. How is their combined probability found?
questions.explanation: Distinct terminal outcomes are disjoint, so their probabilities add.
choices: Ignore one because both describe one head.
Subtract the smaller from the larger.

questions.stem: Normal models share SD 4 but have means 10 and 14. Which has more probability below 8?
questions.explanation: A left cutoff is nearer the center of the mean-10 model.

questions.stem: For an exponential wait, which one-minute interval has more probability?
questions.explanation: An exponential density decreases with waiting time.

figure.alt: A declining exponential density highlights 0 to 1 minute and 5 to 6 minutes.

data.alt: A declining exponential density highlights 0 to 1 minute and 5 to 6 minutes.

questions.stem: A survey records whether each student uses a service. Which summary directly answers how common use is?
questions.explanation: A yes/no question is naturally summarized by its use proportion.

source.slide_title: The terms in a proportion study

choices: The total of category labels chosen arbitrarily.
The proportion of students reporting use.

questions.stem: A question asks for the mass exceeded by only 10% of packages. What units should the answer have?
questions.explanation: The requested answer is an original-scale cutoff, not a probability.
choices: No units because it is a z-score automatically.

questions.stem: A fixed fee increases by 2 dollars. What happens to net-gain mean and SD?
questions.explanation: Subtracting a constant shifts all outcomes without changing their spread.
choices: Mean falls by 2; SD is unchanged.

questions.stem: Students may use both laptops and tablets. Laptop use is 70%, tablet use 60%. Why is a two-slice pie chart inappropriate?
questions.explanation: Pie slices partition a whole; overlapping memberships are not such a partition.
choices: A pie chart requires exactly three categories.

questions.stem: A box has 8 red and 2 blue tokens; 5 are drawn without replacement. What is the minimum red count?
questions.explanation: At most two drawn tokens can be blue, leaving at least three red.

questions.stem: A question asks for the mass exceeded by only 10% of packages. What units should the answer have?
questions.explanation: The requested answer is an original-scale cutoff, not a probability.
choices: No units because it is a z-score automatically.

questions.stem: The course uses N(mean, SD). A technician expects readings from N(40,6) to cluster near 6. What is the best correction?
questions.explanation: The first parameter is the center; the SD measures variation around it, rather than another center.
choices: They cluster near 6; 40 is the sample size.
The model allows only the two values 6 and 40.
The readings cluster near 40; 6 describes their spread.

questions.stem: A sample has 8 observations. Its sum of squared deviations is already supplied. Which divisor gives sample variance?
questions.explanation: Sample variance uses n-1, unlike the population calculation with all population members.

questions.stem: Sample SD is 6 minutes and n=9; sqrt(9)=3. What estimated SE is used?
questions.explanation: Estimated SE is s/sqrt(n) and retains the measurement units.

questions.stem: To find the probability of A followed by B when the stages may be dependent, which expression fits?
questions.explanation: The general multiplication rule uses the appropriate conditional probability.
choices: P(A) times P(B) without checking independence.

questions.stem: Population mean is 20; SE of sample means is 2. An observed sample mean is 24. What standardized distance does it have?
questions.explanation: Its deviation is 4, or 2 standard errors.

questions.stem: Data are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. How do mean and median compare?
questions.explanation: The values balance symmetrically around 6.
choices: The mean is below the median.

questions.stem: A wait is uniform from 0 to 12 minutes. What is P(3<X<6)?
questions.explanation: The interval occupies 3 of the support's 12 minutes.

questions.stem: A normal model has mean 50 and SD 2. Which interval contains about 99.7%?
questions.explanation: The empirical rule uses three SD on each side.

questions.skill_group: Continuous densities, areas, and cumulative probabilities
questions.stem: Durations are rounded to the nearest whole second. Ignoring tie conventions at boundaries, which exact interval reports as 4?
questions.explanation: Nearest-unit rounding collects values within half a unit of 4.

questions.stem: A sample of 6 has strong skewness and an extreme outlier. What is sensible about a t interval?
questions.explanation: The small sample may not support the normality assumptions of the usual t method.
choices: Six observations guarantee a normal sampling distribution.
The outlier must be removed without investigation.
It is automatically reliable because t has heavy tails.

questions.stem: What does a 95% confidence procedure mean in repeated appropriate sampling?
questions.explanation: Confidence describes long-run coverage by the method.
choices: About 95% of intervals constructed this way contain the fixed population mean in the long run.
95% of observations lie in every interval.
The sample mean equals the population mean 95% of the time.
Every interval has 95% of its length below the mean.

questions.stem: X counts failures in exactly 20 independent trials; Y counts arrivals during an hour with no fixed trial total. Which distinction matters?
questions.explanation: A fixed set of trials differs from event counts over an interval.
choices: Both must have the same maximum.
X fits a binomial setting; Y may fit a Poisson setting if its assumptions hold.

questions.stem: A library surveys only people entering the library to estimate how often all students visit. What is the main concern?
questions.explanation: Selection excludes a relevant part of the population, regardless of sample size.
choices: Students who never visit are excluded.
Randomly ordering the responses removes the concern.
The sample must be too small.
Every recorded visit count is wrong.

questions.stem: The ordered data are 1, 3, 5, 9. What is the median?
questions.explanation: Average the two middle values, 3 and 5.

questions.stem: Ten independent trials each have success probability 0.3. X counts successes. What makes a binomial model appropriate?
questions.explanation: Those experimental conditions define the binomial setting.
choices: Fixed trial count, two outcomes, independence, and constant success chance.
The expected count is an integer.

questions.stem: A model allows counts 0,1,2,... without a finite upper limit. Can it still be discrete?
questions.explanation: Discrete support can be infinite without forming a continuum.
choices: No; a count must stop at 10.
Yes; countably many separated values can be discrete.
Only if every count has equal probability.
No; all infinite possibilities are continuous.

questions.stem: The course's binomial normal approximation check requires np>5 and n(1-p)>5. For n=100, p=0.02, which judgment fits?
questions.explanation: Both expected-count requirements must hold.
choices: It passes because p is positive.
It fails because expected failures are 98.
It fails because expected successes are only 2.

questions.stem: Two successes in four trials can occur in several orders. Why must all those orders be considered?
questions.explanation: A count aggregates several distinct trial sequences.
choices: The expected count is an order.
The count event includes every order with two successes.
Different orders are the same elementary outcome.
Only the first successful order can occur.

questions.stem: A recorded file size is far above the rest. What should happen before deleting it?
questions.explanation: An unusual value can be valid and informative; deletion needs a defensible reason.
choices: Check whether it is an error or a genuine unusual file.
Keep it only if the mean equals the median.
Delete it because all outliers are mistakes.

questions.stem: A proportion estimate is 0.40 with margin 0.05. What interval is this in percentages?
questions.explanation: Convert the endpoints 0.35 and 0.45 to percentages.

questions.stem: A grouped table reports 12 durations from 5 to less than 10 seconds. Can it tell exactly how many equal 7 seconds?
questions.explanation: Grouping preserves interval counts but loses individual values.
choices: No; exact positions within the interval are hidden.

questions.stem: After five failures with constant independent p=0.2, what is the chance the next trial succeeds?
questions.explanation: The trial chance stays unchanged; success does not become due.

questions.stem: X is uniform from 0 to 10. Compare intervals 1 to 3 and 7 to 9.
questions.explanation: Under a flat density, equal-length intervals inside the support have equal area.
choices: Their probabilities depend on the sample median.
The second is more likely because its values are larger.
The first is more likely because it is closer to zero.

figure.alt: A uniform density on 0 to 10 highlights intervals 1 to 3 and 7 to 9.

data.alt: A uniform density on 0 to 10 highlights intervals 1 to 3 and 7 to 9.

questions.stem: A shipment contains 36 packages. Which variable answers the question of average mass per package in that shipment?
questions.explanation: The requested average is a statistic across the shipment's packages.

questions.stem: For a standard normal variable, compare P(Z<-1.4) and P(Z>1.4).
questions.explanation: Normal symmetry makes opposite equal-distance tails equal.

questions.stem: A fair six-sided die is rolled. What is the probability of a result greater than 4?
questions.explanation: Only 5 and 6 satisfy the event among six equally likely outcomes.

questions.stem: A 95% mean interval is 10 to 14 minutes. Does this say 95% of individual durations lie there?
questions.explanation: An interval for a parameter is different from an interval covering individual values.
choices: Yes; the mean and individuals have identical spread.
No; it instead guarantees every duration lies there.
Yes; that is the meaning of any confidence interval.
No; it estimates the population mean.

questions.stem: Why is adding signed deviations from the sample mean unsuitable as a spread measure?
questions.explanation: Signed deviations sum to zero even when observations are widely spread.
choices: The mean is always the largest value.
It necessarily counts each value twice.

questions.stem: A dot plot has five dots at 2 visits and one dot at 8 visits. What does the stack at 2 mean?
questions.explanation: Each dot represents an observation; a stack records repeated values.

figure.alt: Five dots at 2 visits and one dot at 8 visits.

data.alt: Five dots at 2 visits and one dot at 8 visits.

questions.stem: Larger independent samples yield less variable means. Does this make individual packages less variable?
questions.explanation: Averaging improves precision of the statistic without changing the population.
choices: Only if more samples are plotted.
No; population spread stays the same.
Yes; every package moves toward the mean.

questions.stem: The slides recommend plus-four when confidence is at least 90% and n>=10. Does n=24 at 85% confidence meet that recommendation?
questions.explanation: Both stated recommendations must be met; this is distinct from the ordinary interval count check.
choices: Yes; plus-four has no stated conditions.
No; the confidence level is below the stated threshold.

questions.stem: Probability is shifted from a low outcome to a higher outcome, with other probabilities unchanged. What happens to expected value?
questions.explanation: Giving more weight to a larger value raises the weighted mean.
choices: It must become the largest outcome.

questions.stem: A uniform interval centered at 10 doubles its width while keeping center 10. What happens?
questions.explanation: Uniform mean depends on midpoint; SD is proportional to width.

questions.stem: A supplied probability table lists P(X=0),...,P(X=8). To find P(X<=2), which entries are needed?
questions.explanation: At most 2 is a cumulative event including all counts through 2.

questions.stem: From the same sample, a 90% and 99% mean interval are built with the same method. Which statement fits?
questions.explanation: Changing confidence changes the critical multiplier, not the observed estimate.
choices: The 99% interval is wider but has the same center.
The 99% interval has a different sample mean.

questions.stem: Mean is 100, SD is 10, and the supplied 90th-percentile z is 1.28. What is the corresponding value?
questions.explanation: Return to original units with mean plus z times SD.

questions.stem: P(A)=0.2 but P(A AND B)=0.3. Why is this impossible?
questions.explanation: The intersection is a subset of A and cannot be more probable than A.
choices: The overlap must always equal zero.
The overlap cannot exceed the probability of A.

questions.stem: A bell-shaped distribution has mean 20 and SD 2. Approximately which interval contains 95%?
questions.explanation: The empirical rule uses about two standard deviations on each side for a bell-shaped distribution.

questions.stem: A proposed normal model gives substantial probability to negative durations. What is the concern?
questions.explanation: A normal approximation may be poor when impossible values receive meaningful probability.
choices: Normal distributions cannot model any positive variable.
It assigns appreciable probability to impossible values.

questions.stem: A distribution gives P(X=0)=0.2 and P(X=1)=0.5, with only X=0,1,2 possible. What is P(X=2)?
questions.explanation: The missing probability makes the total equal to 1.

questions.stem: A sum event and its equivalent mean event use correctly matched centers and SDs. How do their z-scores compare?
questions.explanation: Scaling numerator and denominator by n leaves standardization unchanged.
choices: The mean z-score is always zero.
The sum z-score is n times larger.

questions.stem: For a normal model, where is the 10th percentile?
questions.explanation: The lowest tenth ends on the lower side of the symmetric center.

questions.stem: A supplied exponential model gives P(X>8)=0.20. What is P(X<=8)?
questions.explanation: Meeting the deadline complements exceeding it.

questions.stem: Two reasonable quartile methods give upper outlier fences of 18 and 20 for the same dataset. One observation is 35. Which conclusion agrees with both methods?
questions.explanation: The value 35 is well above both reported fences, so choosing between these conventions does not change the flag. An outlier flag alone does not establish a recording error.
choices: The observation is flagged as unusually high under both methods.
Only the method with fence 18 flags the observation.
The observation must be a recording error.
The observation is not flagged under either method.

questions.stem: For comparison, sample SD and confidence are held fixed while n increases. What happens to a t mean interval's margin?
questions.explanation: Larger n reduces estimated SE and increases degrees of freedom.
choices: It decreases as SE and the critical t value decrease.
It increases because there are more observations.

questions.stem: X counts successes in 8 trials. Which proposed outcome is impossible?
questions.explanation: A success count cannot exceed the fixed number of trials.

questions.stem: A public dataset includes names beside individual survey answers. Which change best protects privacy while preserving group summaries?
questions.explanation: De-identification can preserve useful aggregate evidence while reducing identification risks.
choices: Replace every answer with the overall mean.
Keep names and omit the study methods.

questions.stem: A grader does not know which practice format each paper's author used. What problem does this reduce?
questions.explanation: Blinding the grader reduces assessment bias tied to treatment knowledge.
choices: Students being absent from the population.

questions.stem: Compare one U(0,12) wait with the average of 100 independent such waits. Which is less variable?
questions.explanation: Averaging independent observations reduces variability without fixing the result exactly.
choices: The average must have zero spread.

questions.stem: From the same sample, a 90% and 99% mean interval are built with the same method. Which statement fits?
questions.explanation: Changing confidence changes the critical multiplier, not the observed estimate.
choices: The 99% interval is wider but has the same center.
The 99% interval has a different sample mean.

questions.stem: Mean is 100, SD is 10, and the supplied 90th-percentile z is 1.28. What is the corresponding value?
questions.explanation: Return to original units with mean plus z times SD.

questions.stem: Outcomes 0 and 10 have probabilities 0.9 and 0.1. Why is their expected value not 5?
questions.explanation: The weighted mean is 1, not the unweighted midpoint.
choices: The outcomes require unequal probability weights.
Expected value always equals the most likely outcome.

questions.stem: Which event is the complement of at least one failure in three trials?
questions.explanation: The only way to avoid any failure is to have none.

questions.stem: About 99.7% lies within 3 SD in a normal model. About what percent lies outside on both sides combined?
questions.explanation: The combined outside area is 100%-99.7%.

questions.stem: For a normal population, compare one mass exceeding mean+2 g with the mean of 100 independent masses exceeding the same cutoff. Which is more likely?
questions.explanation: Averaging narrows the distribution around the same center.

questions.stem: For 2, 3, 3, 4, 18, how does the mean compare with the median?
questions.explanation: The high value pulls the mean above the median of 3.
choices: No comparison is possible without a calculator.

questions.stem: Durations are in seconds. Which units belong to variance and standard deviation, respectively?
questions.explanation: Variance averages squared distances; standard deviation takes the square root.

questions.stem: Among 200 recorded jobs, 30 were late. What does 30/200 describe?
questions.explanation: An empirical frequency summarizes observations and can estimate a probability.
choices: A guarantee that the next job is late.
The exact long-run probability under every possible condition.
The number of late jobs that must occur tomorrow.

questions.stem: Most waits are short, but a few extend far toward large values. What determines the skew direction?
questions.explanation: Skew is named for the direction of the long tail.
choices: The long tail toward large values.
The side with the tallest bar alone.

questions.stem: For a bell-shaped normal model, about 68% lies within 1 SD. About how much lies outside that central interval?
questions.explanation: The outside area is the complement, split between two tails.

questions.stem: A report gives 30 successes among 120 observations. Which is the estimate of population success proportion?
questions.explanation: The success count must be divided by the total to estimate the proportion.

questions.stem: A public dataset includes names beside individual survey answers. Which change best protects privacy while preserving group summaries?
questions.explanation: De-identification can preserve useful aggregate evidence while reducing identification risks.
choices: Replace every answer with the overall mean.
Keep names and omit the study methods.

questions.stem: Five print jobs contain 2, 3, 3, 5, and 7 pages. What is the mean number of pages per job?
questions.explanation: The total is 20 pages, and 20 divided by 5 jobs is 4 pages per job.

questions.stem: Ten cables are sampled without replacement from 100,000. Why might binomial be a useful approximation?
questions.explanation: A tiny sampling fraction makes dependence weak, but the exact design remains hypergeometric.
choices: All samples have the same faulty count.
The small sample barely changes the population composition.

questions.stem: A probability interval is widened to include its original interval plus a region of positive density. What happens to its probability?
questions.explanation: Adding positive area raises probability while the total remains at most 1.

questions.stem: Population mean is 20; SE of sample means is 2. An observed sample mean is 24. What standardized distance does it have?
questions.explanation: Its deviation is 4, or 2 standard errors.

questions.stem: Uniform model A spans width 4; model B spans width 8. Which density is taller?
questions.explanation: A narrower rectangular support requires a taller density to preserve total area 1.
choices: The one with the larger mean regardless of width.

questions.stem: Which Venn region is the complement of A OR B?

Whether every observation equals the mean.

questions.stem: Categories in a bar graph are reordered alphabetically. What changes?
questions.explanation: Changing categorical order does not change the observations.
choices: The display order, but not category frequencies.
The number of observations in each category.

questions.stem: For a bell-shaped normal model, about 68% lies within 1 SD. About how much lies outside that central interval?
questions.explanation: The outside area is the complement, split between two tails.

They are impossible once the mean is exceeded.
They are possible but less common than short waits.

questions.stem: A package is accepted if 490<mass<520. Which part of its normal curve should be shaded?
questions.explanation: A between-cutoffs event corresponds to the intervening area.

questions.stem: A mean is estimated from grouped intervals using midpoints. Why is it generally approximate?
questions.explanation: Grouping hides exact values, so midpoint weighting replaces them with approximations.
choices: Frequencies cannot be used in means.
Actual observations need not equal the interval midpoints.
The sample size is necessarily unknown.

questions.stem: A sum distribution has mean 100 and SD 4. What total is 2 SD above its mean?
questions.explanation: Add two times the sum's SD to its mean.

questions.stem: A uniform wait ranges from 0 to 10. Only 10% exceed a cutoff. Where is that cutoff?
questions.explanation: The uppermost tenth of the support is 9 to 10.

questions.stem: Game A pays 5 with certainty. Game B pays 0 or 10 with equal chance. What is true?
questions.explanation: Both means are 5, but only B varies from play to play.
choices: They have equal expected payout; B has greater spread.
B has a larger expected payout.

questions.stem: A supplied positive critical z leaves 0.025 to its right. What cumulative area lies to its left?
questions.explanation: Left and right areas total 1.

questions.stem: The plus-four estimate adds two successes and two failures. With 8 successes out of 40, what adjusted fraction is used?
questions.explanation: The adjusted count is x+2 and the adjusted total is n+4.

questions.stem: Students may use both laptops and tablets. Laptop use is 70%, tablet use 60%. Why is a two-slice pie chart inappropriate?
questions.explanation: Pie slices partition a whole; overlapping memberships are not such a partition.
choices: A pie chart requires exactly three categories.

questions.stem: A fixed 5-kg container is added to a shipment of random item masses. What changes?
questions.explanation: A fixed additive quantity shifts the distribution without adding random variability.
choices: Expected total rises by 5 kg; total SD is unchanged.
Both mean and SD rise by 5 kg.

questions.stem: After a specific interval is computed, what is correct about its relation to a fixed population mean?
questions.explanation: Frequentist coverage refers to random intervals before observing the data.
choices: It either contains that mean or does not; 95% describes the procedure.
The fixed mean changes to fit it with probability 95%.
The mean occupies 95% of the interval.
The endpoints must equal the smallest and largest observation.

questions.stem: Which design permits an exact binomial count model with independent randomized draws?
questions.explanation: Replacement and remixing preserve the same independent success chance.
choices: Drawing most of a small population without replacement.
Replacing and remixing each drawn token.
Drawing without replacement until the box is empty.

questions.stem: Among 20 tablet users, 12 also use laptops. What is P(laptop given tablet) in this sample?
questions.explanation: Conditioning restricts the denominator to tablet users.

questions.stem: A file is 60 KB; its group has mean 50 KB and SD 5 KB. How far above the mean is it?
questions.explanation: The difference is 10 KB, or twice the 5 KB standard deviation.

questions.stem: Q1 is 8 and Q3 is 14. What does the interval 8 to 14 describe approximately?
questions.explanation: Quartiles bound approximately the middle 50%, with ties and conventions affecting exact counts.

questions.stem: A payout variable is measured in dollars. What units belong to its variance?
questions.explanation: Variance uses squared deviations from the expected payout.

questions.stem: Independent tasks each succeed with probability 0.9. Which shortcut gives at least one failure among three tasks?
questions.explanation: At least one failure complements all successes.
choices: 1 minus the probability exactly one succeeds.
1 minus the probability all three succeed.

questions.stem: A frequency table lists 1 page for 8 jobs and 5 pages for 2 jobs. Why is (1+5)/2 inappropriate for mean pages per job?
questions.explanation: A per-job mean must weight values by their frequencies.
choices: It counts too many individual jobs.
It ignores how often each value occurs.
It gives extra weight to 1-page jobs.

questions.stem: The course uses N(mean, SD). A technician expects readings from N(40,6) to cluster near 6. What is the best correction?
questions.explanation: The first parameter is the center; the SD measures variation around it, rather than another center.
choices: The model allows only the two values 6 and 40.
The readings cluster near 40; 6 describes their spread.
They cluster near 6; 40 is the sample size.

questions.stem: What equation describes a continuous model's 90th percentile k?
questions.explanation: The percentile cutoff has the stated area to its left.

questions.stem: A uniform wait ranges from 0 to 10. Only 10% exceed a cutoff. Where is that cutoff?
questions.explanation: The uppermost tenth of the support is 9 to 10.

questions.stem: Three reported percentages are 33.3%, 33.3%, and 33.3%. What most reasonably explains the 99.9% total?
questions.explanation: Rounding can make displayed percentages differ slightly from 100%.

questions.stem: At fixed n and confidence, known population SD doubles. What happens to interval width?
questions.explanation: Margin and full width are proportional to population SD.

questions.stem: A population has mean 50. Where are unbiased random-sample means centered?
questions.explanation: The expected sample mean equals the population mean under the sampling assumptions.

questions.stem: A researcher takes 1,000 samples of 25 packages and plots each sample mean. What does one plotted value represent?
questions.explanation: A sampling distribution records a statistic from each repeated sample.
choices: A population parameter that changes on each sample.
The mean of all 25,000 packages combined.

questions.stem: A rate estimate rises from 40% to 45%. What is its increase in percentage points?
questions.explanation: Percentage-point difference subtracts the percentages directly, unlike relative percent increase.

questions.stem: Mean is 30 and SD is 4. Which value has z=1.5?
questions.explanation: Add 1.5 times 4 to the mean.

questions.stem: For a normal model, where is the 10th percentile?
questions.explanation: The lowest tenth ends on the lower side of the symmetric center.

questions.stem: A survey records whether each student uses a service. Which summary directly answers how common use is?
questions.explanation: A yes/no question is naturally summarized by its use proportion.

source.slide_title: The terms in a proportion study

choices: The proportion of students reporting use.
The total of category labels chosen arbitrarily.

questions.stem: Compare 4, 5, 6 with 1, 5, 9. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Both center at 5; the second has observations farther from the center.
choices: They have equal means, but the second has more spread.
The second has a larger mean.

questions.stem: A modified box plot marks 30 as a separate high outlier. Its upper whisker ends at 18. What does 18 represent?
questions.explanation: Modified whiskers end at observed nonoutlier values; the outlier remains part of the data.
choices: The upper fence whether observed or not.
The largest observed value not flagged as an outlier.

questions.stem: A machine's success chance steadily falls as it warms. Which binomial requirement is questionable?
questions.explanation: Changing trial probabilities undermine the common-p binomial model.

questions.skill_group: Continuous densities, areas, and cumulative probabilities
questions.stem: F(3)=0.20 and F(7)=0.80 for a continuous variable. What is P(3<X<7)?
questions.explanation: Subtract the cumulative areas at the two cutoffs.

questions.stem: Two distinct terminal paths describe exactly one head in two tosses. How is their combined probability found?
questions.explanation: Distinct terminal outcomes are disjoint, so their probabilities add.
choices: Ignore one because both describe one head.
Subtract the smaller from the larger.

questions.stem: All ten observations equal 5, so their median is 5. Are exactly half strictly below the median?
questions.explanation: Ties mean a median need not have half the values strictly below it.
choices: No; none are strictly below it.
No; a median cannot exist with ties.
Yes; every median splits strict inequalities equally.

questions.stem: A researcher deletes genuine results that disagree with the desired conclusion. What is the problem?
questions.explanation: Valid observations cannot be discarded merely because they are unfavorable.
choices: A smaller dataset guarantees less bias.
Deleting inconvenient values always improves accuracy.
Any unusual observation is automatically an error.
The report no longer fairly represents the collected evidence.

questions.stem: A proposed normal model gives substantial probability to negative durations. What is the concern?
questions.explanation: A normal approximation may be poor when impossible values receive meaningful probability.
choices: Normal distributions cannot model any positive variable.
It assigns appreciable probability to impossible values.

questions.stem: A fair die is rolled. A means even; B means 6. Why are these events dependent?
questions.explanation: Fair outcomes within one roll do not imply independent events on that roll.
choices: A fair die makes all events independent.
Knowing B guarantees A, changing its probability.

questions.stem: X counts broken cables in independent checks. Can broken be called success in a binomial model?
questions.explanation: Success is a modeling label, not a value judgment.
choices: Only if no cables are broken.
Only if more than half are broken.
Yes; success means the counted outcome.

questions.stem: A distribution has equal peaks near 2 and 8 and is symmetric around 5. What follows?
questions.explanation: A symmetric distribution can be bimodal with its center between peaks.
choices: Symmetry does not require a single peak.

questions.stem: One hundred valid 95% intervals are constructed in repeated sampling. Must exactly 95 cover the mean?
questions.explanation: A long-run proportion is not an exact finite-sample quota.
choices: No; the coverage count itself can vary.
Yes; any other count proves bias.
Yes; the confidence level fixes that count.

questions.stem: The 95th percentile of a sample-mean distribution is 14. What does it describe?
questions.explanation: The percentile belongs to the sampling distribution, not automatically the individual distribution.
choices: 95% of all individuals must be at most 14.
About 95% of repeated sample means are at most 14.

questions.stem: The model changes from U(0,10) to U(0,20). What happens to P(X<5)?
questions.explanation: The favorable interval retains width 5 while total support width doubles.

questions.stem: A normal model's mean rises by 3 with SD fixed. What happens to its 90th percentile?
questions.explanation: Every fixed percentile shifts with the mean when spread stays fixed.

questions.stem: A mean is estimated from grouped intervals using midpoints. Why is it generally approximate?
questions.explanation: Grouping hides exact values, so midpoint weighting replaces them with approximations.
choices: Actual observations need not equal the interval midpoints.
The sample size is necessarily unknown.
Frequencies cannot be used in means.

questions.stem: About 99.7% lies within 3 SD in a normal model. About what percent lies outside on both sides combined?
questions.explanation: The combined outside area is 100%-99.7%.

questions.stem: A first branch has probability 0.4; its next conditional branch is 0.5. What is the path probability?
questions.explanation: Multiply probabilities along a path.

questions.stem: The course's ordinary normal-approximation interval check requires more than 5 observed successes and more than 5 failures. Which sample passes?
questions.explanation: Both observed counts must exceed 5 under the stated convention.

questions.stem: What equation describes a continuous model's 90th percentile k?
questions.explanation: The percentile cutoff has the stated area to its left.

questions.stem: Four mutually exclusive, exhaustive categories have reported proportions 0.20, 0.30, 0.40, and 0.25. What needs checking?
questions.explanation: Exhaustive nonoverlapping categories must have total probability or relative frequency 1.

questions.stem: A population has mean 50. Where are unbiased random-sample means centered?
questions.explanation: The expected sample mean equals the population mean under the sampling assumptions.

questions.stem: A sample variance is 9 minutes squared. What is its standard deviation?
questions.explanation: Standard deviation is the square root of variance and returns to the original units.

questions.stem: A fixed fee increases by 2 dollars. What happens to net-gain mean and SD?
questions.explanation: Subtracting a constant shifts all outcomes without changing their spread.
choices: Mean falls by 2; SD is unchanged.

questions.stem: Arrival rates sharply rise at lunchtime. What is questionable about a single exponential waiting model over the whole day?
questions.explanation: The homogeneous exponential waiting model relies on a stable Poisson-process rate.
choices: A constant rate across the whole period.

questions.skill_group: Continuous densities, areas, and cumulative probabilities
questions.stem: A proposed density dips below zero over an interval. What is wrong?
questions.explanation: Nonnegative density is required for nonnegative interval probabilities.
choices: Every valid density must be symmetric.
It would assign negative area to that interval.
A density must be flat everywhere.

questions.stem: Population SD doubles while sample size stays fixed. What happens to SE?
questions.explanation: SE is proportional to population SD at fixed n.

questions.stem: A box has 4 red and 6 blue tokens; 3 are drawn without replacement. What red counts are possible?
questions.explanation: The count ranges from zero through the sample size, within population limits.

questions.stem: Everyone tries format A first and format B second. What could explain better second scores besides format B?
questions.explanation: Order and practice can be confounded with format.
choices: The lack of any treatment order.
A guarantee of equal prior knowledge.

questions.stem: A model predicts 5% of items fall outside specifications. Among 200 items, how many are expected outside?
questions.explanation: Expected count is sample count times the modeled fraction, without a guarantee.

questions.stem: Durations are in seconds. Which units belong to variance and standard deviation, respectively?
questions.explanation: Variance averages squared distances; standard deviation takes the square root.

questions.stem: A model allows counts 0,1,2,... without a finite upper limit. Can it still be discrete?
questions.explanation: Discrete support can be infinite without forming a continuum.
choices: Only if every count has equal probability.
Yes; countably many separated values can be discrete.
No; all infinite possibilities are continuous.
No; a count must stop at 10.

questions.stem: A strongly skewed variable is converted to z-scores. Does it become normal?
questions.explanation: A linear transformation preserves distributional shape.
choices: No; standardization shifts and rescales without removing skew.
Yes; subtracting the mean removes the tail.
Yes; every z-score distribution is standard normal.

questions.stem: A score is reported at approximately the 90th percentile. What kind of information does that give?
questions.explanation: A percentile describes relative position, not percentage correct. This question does not require an exact rank, tie rule, or interpolation convention.
choices: That 90% of exam answers were correct.
Its position relative to other scores.

questions.stem: A sample has 2 successes and 98 failures. Does a large total alone justify the ordinary normal-approximation proportion interval?
questions.explanation: The success-failure check concerns both counts, not just total n.
choices: No; proportions cannot be estimated at all.
No; the observed success count is too sparse.

questions.stem: The number of independent items rises from 25 to 100. What happens to expected sum and SD of sum?
questions.explanation: Sum mean scales with n and sum SD with sqrt(n).
choices: Expected sum stays fixed; SD halves.

questions.stem: A proposed event probability is 1.15. What is wrong?
questions.explanation: Probability measures a fraction of total chance and lies between 0 and 1.

questions.stem: A fixed fee increases by 2 dollars. What happens to net-gain mean and SD?
questions.explanation: Subtracting a constant shifts all outcomes without changing their spread.
choices: Mean falls by 2; SD is unchanged.

questions.stem: Which question targets a population proportion?
questions.explanation: A proportion summarizes membership in a defined yes/no outcome.
choices: What is the SD of file sizes?
What fraction of jobs finish on time?
What is the median number of pages?
What is the mean duration of jobs?

questions.stem: Durations are in seconds. Which units belong to variance and standard deviation, respectively?
questions.explanation: Variance averages squared distances; standard deviation takes the square root.

questions.stem: A recorded file size is far above the rest. What should happen before deleting it?
questions.explanation: An unusual value can be valid and informative; deletion needs a defensible reason.
choices: Keep it only if the mean equals the median.
Delete it because all outliers are mistakes.
Check whether it is an error or a genuine unusual file.

questions.skill_group: Continuous densities, areas, and cumulative probabilities
questions.stem: A continuous model has F(9)=0.80. What percent exceeds 9?
questions.explanation: The upper tail complements the cumulative probability.

questions.stem: Mean is 30 and SD is 4. Which value has z=1.5?
questions.explanation: Add 1.5 times 4 to the mean.

questions.stem: A room at 20 degrees Celsius is compared with one at 10 degrees Celsius. Which statement is justified?
questions.explanation: Celsius supports meaningful differences but its zero is not an absolute zero.
choices: The first has twice the absolute temperature.
The first is 10 degrees warmer on that scale.
The first is twice as comfortable for every person.

questions.stem: P(Z>1.2)=0.1151. By symmetry, what is P(Z<-1.2)?
questions.explanation: Opposite equal-distance tails have equal positive probability.

questions.stem: Requests follow a constant-rate Poisson process at 4 per hour. What is the mean waiting time to the next request?
questions.explanation: Mean wait is one quarter hour, or 15 minutes.

questions.stem: A stemplot key says stem 2, leaf 5 means 25 KB. Stem 3 has leaves 0, 2, 2. Which values does it show?
questions.explanation: The key supplies place value and repeated leaves represent repeated observations.

questions.stem: Data are 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. How do mean and median compare?
questions.explanation: The values balance symmetrically around 6.
choices: The mean is below the median.

questions.stem: A symmetric interval is 8 to 12. What is the margin of error?
questions.explanation: Margin of error is half the total width.

questions.stem: P(X>50)=0.50 and P(X>60)=0.10. Given X>50, what is P(X>60)?
questions.explanation: The smaller upper-tail event is contained in the conditioned event, giving 0.10/0.50.

questions.stem: P(A OR B)=0.75. What is the probability of neither?
questions.explanation: Neither is the complement of the union.

questions.stem: Compare 4, 5, 6 with 1, 5, 9. Which statement is correct?
questions.explanation: Both center at 5; the second has observations farther from the center.
choices: They have equal means, but the second has more spread.
The second has a larger mean.

questions.stem: An exponential population has mean 5. Which is generally more unusual under independent sampling: one duration above 7 or 100 durations averaging above 7?
questions.explanation: The average is far less variable around the same mean.

questions.stem: A supplied normal table gives P(Z<1.2)=0.8849. What is P(Z>1.2)?
questions.explanation: Use the complement for the upper tail.

questions.stem: Which variable is a count rather than a waiting time?
questions.explanation: A Poisson variable counts events in an interval; a waiting time is a different variable.
choices: Requests received in the next five minutes.
